info.name: Server Moderation Session Service
info.description:
Team 16 - "Student ID, please". Server Moderation Session Service, owner Postoronca Dumitru.

Every request name carries the status code it expects, so the collection can be checked mechanically. Folders marked 'run in order' capture ids into collection variables and depend on the requests before them - use the Collection Runner on the folder rather than firing individual requests.

Order: health -> sessions (contract) -> dev - decision.recorded -> ending the shift -> errors - setup -> error codes -> sessions (beyond contract) -> cleanup.

Requests that act for a player send `Authorization: Bearer <jwt>` - an unsigned, JWT-shaped token carrying the player id as its `sub` claim, which is what University Record Service also accepts. The collection's pre-request script mints them, so there is nothing to set up. `X-Player-Id` still works as a fallback; see the 'caller identity' folder.

Set `base_url` if the service is not on http://localhost:8088. The player ids are pre-filled with the ones Player Service seeds, so they resolve whether this service is pointed at the real Player Service or using its built-in stub.

Full reference: docs/SERVER_MODERATION_SESSION_SERVICE.md in the Common Public Repository.

item.name: health
item.description: The liveness and readiness pair every service in the system exposes, outside /api/v1.

request.description: Liveness. Never consults a dependency: a database blip must not make an orchestrator restart a container that is running fine.
Readiness. Reports Postgres plus each of the three services this one calls, saying which are real ('configured') and which are answered in-process ('stub').

item.name: caller identity
item.description:
Proves how this service decides which player a request acts for, without creating anything: each request either fails authentication outright, or gets past it to a Player Service lookup that 404s. Safe to run at any point.

The primary mechanism is `Authorization: Bearer <jwt>` with the player id in the `sub` claim, unverified - matching University Record Service. `X-Player-Id` is kept as a fallback because a bare UUID is easier to type into curl than a JWT.

item.name: Bearer token for an unknown player -> 404 PLAYER_NOT_FOUND

request.description: A 404 rather than a 401 is the proof: the token was read and its `sub` claim was taken as the caller, then Player Service was asked about that player and did not know them.

exec: pm.test('404 - the token was read', () => pm.response.to.have.status(404));

item.name: X-Player-Id fallback for an unknown player -> 404 PLAYER_NOT_FOUND

request.description: The same proof for the fallback header.

exec: pm.test('404 - the fallback header was read', () => pm.response.to.have.status(404));

request.description: 401 rather than 400: the request is well formed, it simply says nothing about who is making it - which is the status a real token check would return too.

item.name: a token that is not JWT-shaped -> 401

request.description: A token present but unusable is refused rather than falling through to the fallback header: silently masking a bad token with a stale id would make the failure impossible to diagnose.
Only the Bearer scheme is accepted (case-insensitively, per RFC 7235).

item.name: dev - decision.recorded (mocks Moderation Service)
item.description: Moderation Service has not been written, and the team is writing its own message broker to replace RabbitMQ, so nothing delivers decision.recorded. This endpoint accepts the exact envelope a broker would carry and runs it through the same handler a broker client will call. It is mounted only when ENABLE_DEV_ENDPOINTS is true, and it moves a session's score with no credential - so it is off outside a demo.

request.description: A correct decision adds SCORE_PER_CORRECT * difficulty to the score, increments applications_processed, and marks the current applicant decided so the Moderator may ask for the next one.

item.name: 2. POST the SAME event again -> 200 duplicate:true

request.description: The contract requires every consumer to dedupe by event_id, because an event may be delivered more than once. A replay is a success, not an error - and the 'duplicate' flag is how a caller can see the deduplication fire. Run request 1 and this one, then check the session: the counters must have moved once.

exec: pm.test('200 - a replay is a success', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));
